own_scenes.family: Nueva York: Def Jam, Queens y la edad de oro
own_scenes.desc: Christopher Wallace, hijo de una jamaicana que trabajaba en dos empleos para pagarle el colegio, era Peter Parker en casa y Spider-Man en la esquina; dejó los estudios por el trapicheo, pasó nueve meses en la cárcel y su maqueta con 50 Grand llegó a Mister Cee y a la columna Unsigned Hype de Matty C: «el segundo advenimiento de Kane con la voz de KRS». Sean «Puff Daddy» Combs, bailarín de Heavy D y becario de Uptown con Andre Harrell, había inventado el hip-hop soul (las mezclas de R&B y breaks para Jodeci y Mary J. Blige); despedido en 1993, se quedó a Biggie y fundó Bad Boy con Arista, y lo sacó de Carolina del Norte horas antes de una redada. Como Belichick y Brady, la tensión los hacía mejores: Biggie no escribía nada; Puff le pedía éxitos sobre hits de los ochenta («Juicy» sobre Mtume, «Big Poppa» sobre los Isley) para vender a las mujeres sin perder la dureza. Ready to Die (septiembre de 1994) rompió el dominio del Oeste; antes «Flava in Ya Ear» de Craig Mack había abierto camino. Biggie colocó a Junior M.A.F.I.A. y a Lil’ Kim; Mary J. Blige, reina del hip-hop soul, le trajo a The Lox. Los Hitmen (D-Dot, Nashiem Myrick, Carlos Broady, Stevie J, Chucky Thompson…), en parejas que competían, samplearon soul de Memphis y en Trinidad grabaron No Way Out y Life After Death. Biggie murió tiroteado en Los Ángeles el 9 de marzo de 1997, con veinticuatro años; el doble disco salió dos semanas después. Su sueño de convertir la cultura en negocio lo cumplió Jay-Z.

refs.q: Christopher Wallace was Peter Parker and on the streets he was Spider-Man.
refs.para: Cheo Hodari Coker (journalist): Biggie was a stoop kid who became a corner kid. Voletta Wallace was strict—Jehovah’s Witness, Jamaican, “Do your homework.” So, at home, that’s what his life was. And then he would go out on the corner with his friends, and he basically had two different lives. Christopher Wallace was Peter Parker and on the streets he was Spider-Man. And his whole fear was that Aunt May would find out.

refs.q: Their relationship was like [Bill] Belichick and [Tom] Brady.
refs.para: Their relationship was like [Bill] Belichick and [Tom] Brady. They brought things out of each other. Their tension is what made it work. It was tension like, “You’re a pain in my ass, but fine, I’ll do it your way”—on both sides. So, the same way that Belichick has a structure and basically created the Patriot Way, in which it allows the 199th pick of the draft to become the greatest quarterback of all time, at the same time, the quarterback, his prodigious talent, is what makes the system work. That’s what Biggie and Puff were like.

refs.q: The money wasn’t in hip-hop; the money was in monetizing the culture of hip-hop—that’s what makes you a billionaire.
refs.para: At the same time, there was also a certain entrepreneurial sense, because I think Big, had he been able to live up to his potential, he definitely would’ve been trying to do exactly what Jay-Z ended up doing, which is maintaining hip-hop relevance and making records when he wants to make records, but then at the same time, making business moves. Everybody thought for a long time that the money was in hip-hop. The money wasn’t in hip-hop; the money was in monetizing the culture of hip-hop—that’s what makes you a billionaire.
